podcast.title: Name Acquisition from Liverpool Band (October 2002) – $30,000 Payment
podcast.body: The American supergroup faced a challenge when they chose the name "Audioslave," only to discover a Liverpool band already using it. After an initial offer of $5,000 was rejected, the American band's managers eventually paid the Liverpool group $30,000 in late October 2002 for the rights to the name, just weeks before their debut album's release. "In the end, they were paid $30,000 to go away. Liverpool AudioSlave changed their name to the most terrifying thing."

podcast.title: Rebirth from Rage Against the Machine (Pre-2005)
podcast.body: The band was formed as a "rebirth" of Rage Against the Machine, with Chris Cornell of Soundgarden taking on vocal duties, becoming one of the successful acts in the mid-2000s rock revival. "Raged against the machinehead, more or less been reborn as audio slave with Chris Cornell of Soundguard doing the singing."

podcast.title: "Civilian" Demos – Early, Unofficial Name
podcast.body: Before Audioslave officially formed, 13 demos featuring Chris Cornell with the Rage Against the Machine instrumentalists surfaced online under the name "Civilian." This name was considered for the band but was ultimately found to be already taken. "It was then that 13 demos showed up online under the name civilian."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Audioslave Formed After Rick Rubin Suggested Chris Cornell; Be Real of Cypress Hill Also Auditioned
podcast.body: After Zack de la Rocha quit Rage Against the Machine in 2000, the remaining three members tried to continue under the RATM name with a new singer. Be Real of Cypress Hill auditioned. But after some jamming, they decided they didn't want a Zack sound-alike — they wanted something new. Producer Rick Rubin suggested they talk to ex-Soundgarden singer Chris Cornell. The chemistry was immediate. They began writing as "Civilian" or "the Civilian project" but had to rename when they discovered another group was using that name. They chose Audioslave. The group was essentially Rage with a different singer, and they were productive from 2001 through 2007. "The chemistry was immediate."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Authenticity of "Audioslave" Album Cover
podcast.body: The cover artwork for Audioslave's 2002 debut album is notable for its authentic production, being a genuine, posed photograph captured in a real-world location on the volcanic island of Lanzarote, one of the Canary Islands. The design deliberately eschewed modern digital manipulation, meaning "there's no photoshop. There's no AI" involved in its creation. "Now what I love about covers like this is that there's no photoshop. There's no AI. This is a posed photograph in a real location."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Black Calivados – Chris Cornell's Parisian Restaurant
podcast.body: Chris Cornell invested in and owned a restaurant in Paris named Black Calivados, which he opened around the time he fell in love with publicist Vicki Cariannis, daughter of a New York restaurant executive. The restaurant is described as "very hip, very expensive," with decor designed by the individual responsible for Victoria's Secret fashion shows. The menu offers "New American" cuisine, featuring dishes like Caramelized Quail, Truffled Mac and Cheese, and Peanut Butter, Soul, and Popcorn Fois Gras, with a burger priced at approximately 40 euros. "But modeling is a fickle thing, so Chris decided to sink money into a restaurant in Paris called Black Calivados."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Censored Alternative Cover for "Audioslave"
podcast.body: During the creative process for Audioslave's debut album, an alternative cover featuring a naked man shot from behind was considered. However, due to concerns about American sensibilities and potential censorship, the decision was made not to use this version for the album's release in the United States. "The cloth figure was nearly replaced by a naked man shot from behind, but America being America, the decision was made not to show any new."

podcast.title: Chris Cornell's Initial Reaction to Jamming
podcast.body: Chris Cornell arrived at the initial rehearsal with a "pretty cavalier attitude," expecting to know within 10 minutes if the collaboration would work. He realized it would be great almost immediately but stayed for an hour and a half before confirming his commitment to forming a band, despite the others wanting to continue jamming. They quickly developed seven songs within a couple of days. "Within 10 minutes, I knew that it would be great. But I stuck in there for maybe an hour and a half. And then they were ready to just keep going and keep going."

podcast.title: Chris Cornell's Pre-Music Career in Seafood and Culinary Arts
podcast.body: Before his musical career, Chris Cornell worked as a fish cutter for a seafood wholesaler in Seattle, where his responsibilities included gutting fish. He eventually advanced his culinary skills to become a sous chef at Ray's Boat House, a restaurant also located in Seattle. "Back before the whole music thing happened, he worked cutting up fish for a seafood wholesaler in Seattle."

podcast.title: Formation from Legendary Bands
podcast.body: Audioslave was formed from the ashes of two prominent bands, Soundgarden and Rage Against the Machine, and quickly achieved significant commercial and critical success. "Audio Slave, which rose out of the ashes of both Soundgarden and Rage against the Machine, and were on the road to releasing three consecutive platinum albums, as well as winning a series of Grammy Awards."

podcast.title: Formation from Rage Against The Machine Members
podcast.body: This band was formed when Chris Cornell joined the remaining three members of Rage Against The Machine (Tom Morello, Timmy, and Brad) after their singer Zack de la Rocha left. The group decided to change their name from Rage Against The Machine to Audioslave. "Tom Morello on the line. And I'm not really sure why there was a collective decision to jettison the Rage name in favor of Audio Slive, which is where we are today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation from Rage Against the Machine Remnants – Producer's Suggestion
podcast.body: Audioslave formed when the remaining members of Rage Against the Machine (Tom Morello, Tim Commerford, Brad Wilk) sought a new singer after Zack de la Rocha's departure. Producer Rick Rubin suggested Chris Cornell, leading to an instant creative connection and the rapid composition of 21 songs. "Rage Against the Machine had imploded... All they needed to do was find a new singer... Then producer Rick Rubin suggested that they ring up Chris Cornell."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation of the Band
podcast.body: After Zach de la Rocha left Rage Against the Machine, the remaining instrumentalists (Tom Morello, Brad Wilk, Timmy C) considered finding a new singer for Rage but were ultimately connected with Chris Cornell by producer Rick Rubin. During their first rehearsals, the immediate chemistry led to the writing of 21 songs in 19 days, including "Exploder," "Light My Way," and "Bring 'Em Back Alive." The members were committed to forming a full band, not just a one-off project, aiming for their new work to be "the best thing" they had ever done. "The first time we got together, we just jammed together and we decided, well, let's just try writing some songs. And I think the first three days of rehearsal with Chris, we wrote, exploder, light my way, and bring them back alive."

podcast.title: Symbolism of "Audioslave" Album Cover
podcast.body: Storm Thorgerson, designer of Audioslave's 2002 debut album cover, explained its profound symbolism. Set on the volcanic island of Lanzarote, the large metal sculpture resembling flames represents "the eternal flame, or the flame of remembrance," embodying the collective memory of the band's two previous incarnations, Soundgarden and Rage Against the Machine. The solitary figure in the landscape represents "pilgrims or slaves of sound." "The flame is the eternal flame, or the flame of remembrance, embodying the memory of two previous incarnations, namely Soundgarden and Rage Against the Machine."

xref.title: Implosion (October 18, 2000) – Zack de la Rocha's Departure
xref.body: Rage Against the Machine experienced an "implosion" on October 18, 2000, when their singer, Zack de la Rocha, quit the band. Despite this, the remaining three members—Tom Morello, Tim Commerford, and Brad Wilk—decided to stay together and search for a new vocalist, leading to the formation of Audioslave. "Singer and Zacti La Roca quit the band on October 18, 2000, and frankly, that was fine as far as the other three guys were concerned. They planned to stay together."

xref.title: Name Sold for $30,000 (October 2002) – To American Supergroup
xref.body: A group from Liverpool already named Audioslave was approached by the managers of the American supergroup (Chris Cornell with Rage Against the Machine's instrumentalists) to acquire their name. After initially rejecting a $5,000 offer, they were eventually paid $30,000 in late October 2002, just weeks before the American band's album release. "The managers rang them up and offered them $5,000 for their name. That seemed a little cheap, so they said no. And so the number went up and up and up. But since this was late October 2002, and the American AudioSlave album was set to be released in less than three weeks, the Liverpool AudioSlave knew they had the upper hand. In the end, they were paid $30,000 to go away."

xref.title: "Arm the Homeless Electric" Guitar
xref.body: His most famous guitar is a custom instrument called the "Arm the Homeless Electric," a slogan he carved into its body in the early 1990s. He purchased the wood body from a luthier in Hollywood in 1986, then customized all its components to his liking, making it his main guitar except during his Audioslave period. "His most famous is probably a custom job that he calls his Arm the Homeless Electric. He calls it this because he carved that slogan, Arm the Homeless, into the body of a guitar sometime in the early 1990s."

xref.title: Audioslave Manager Conflict – Near Breakup
xref.body: The new group, which would become Audioslave, faced immediate challenges when their respective managers began brawling, causing the band to break up before playing their first gig. This administrative hurdle required both managers to be fired and a new management group to be brought in to resolve the issues. "Well, the new group broke up before they played their first gig because the two managers started brawling, and it looked like Rage Against the Machine version 2.0 was dead before it got a chance to do anything."

xref.title: Desire for Hip-Hop Stardom
xref.body: After years as the singer for Soundgarden and Audioslave and releasing rock solo records, Chris Cornell decided he wanted to be a hip-hop star. He pursued this by working with producer Timbaland on his third solo album. "Chris was convinced that drum machines and R&B grooves and samples was the way to go."
